ruleset.name: joke
ruleset.description:
Custom PMD rules for Java. This file is the catalogue: every rule is declared here with its implementing class and documentation. Reference individual rules from it, or take all of them at once through rulesets/java/joke.xml.
Nothing here references a PMD stock category, so this file resolves identically under every PMD 7 version.

rule.name: UseVarForLocalVariables
rule.message: Use ''var'' instead of an explicit local variable type.
rule.description:
Local variable declarations should use `var` where it compiles and preserves the declared type. Repeating a type the compiler already knows adds no information and makes a declaration harder to change.
The rule reports single-variable local declarations, including the variables of basic and enhanced for loops and of try-with-resources.
It deliberately does not report declarations that `var` cannot express: a declaration with no initializer, one initialized to `null`, one using array-initializer shorthand, one initialized with a lambda or a method reference, and one declaring more than one variable. Fields and method, constructor, catch and lambda parameters are out of scope entirely.

rule.name: StaticMethodsModifyStaticState
rule.message: A ''static'' method must write private static state, belong to a utility class, or be a named constructor.
rule.description:
A `static` method should exist only to write class-level state. Anything else is an instance method.
This is about what the modifier tells a reader, not about mocking — Mockito's inline mock maker and Spock's `SpyStatic` both mock statics, so a mockability argument would simply be false. Left unconstrained, `static` means any of five things — helper, factory, constant accessor, entry point, class-state mutator — and therefore means nothing. Under this rule it means exactly one thing, and seeing it tells you to go find the field.
A method is accepted when it writes a private static field: a plain assignment, a compound assignment, an increment or a decrement. A read is not a write — a static method that only returns a private static field is an accessor whose encapsulation was already fake, and the field should have been public. A mutating call such as `REGISTRY.put(k, v)` is not a write either, because nothing can tell `put` from `size`. It follows that a `private static final` field can never justify a static method, since a final field is only ever assigned in its initializer.
A utility class is also accepted: one that declares no instance methods and no public or protected constructor. A class declaring no constructor at all is judged on its implicit one, which takes the class's own access — so a `public class` with no declared constructor is not a utility class. An interface has no constructor, and an enum's implicit constructor is always private.
A type carrying an annotation named `UtilityClass` — Lombok's, or any other — is accepted without the structural test. Lombok privatises the constructor and makes every member static during annotation processing, so the source PMD reads declares instance-looking methods and no constructor at all, which fails both halves of that test on a type that is a utility class once compiled. The annotation is matched by simple name only, so nothing here depends on Lombok being present.
A named constructor is accepted: a `static` method whose declared return type is its own declaring type, or an interface that type directly declares it implements. A test double over such a factory could only return what the constructor it wraps already returns, so there is nothing to intercept. A superclass return type, or an interface inherited transitively rather than declared here, is still reported — that shape is a factory for something else, which is a helper. `void`, a primitive and an array name no such type and are reported too.
The comparison is on simple names, with no type resolution: resolution needs an `auxclasspath` that consumers frequently do not configure, and a misconfigured one would make the rule silently pass. The cost is that a factory returning a same-named type from another package is exempted as well. That trade is deliberate — a missed report review can catch beats silent under-reporting nobody can see.
`main(String[])` and `@BeforeAll` / `@AfterAll` methods are exempt, because the platform forces them to be static and a violation nobody can fix is worse than one that is missed. A `@MethodSource` provider is not exempt — the annotation names it in a string, so nothing can pick it out of the other static methods — and neither is a Spring `static @Bean`. Suppress those at the site.

rule.name: AvoidPrivateAndProtectedMethods
rule.message: Methods must be ''public'' or package-private; a ''protected'' method must declare its intent, and ''private'' is never allowed.
rule.description:
The legal method visibilities are `public`, package-private, and a `protected` that declares why.
A `private` method cannot be reached from a test, so it is only ever exercised through whatever public method calls it: a failure deep in the chain surfaces as a failure of the caller, and it cannot be stubbed when the caller is the thing you meant to test. No annotation changes that, so no marker excuses a `private` method.
`protected` is reachable but is usually the wrong seam. It widens the API to every subclass in every consumer's codebase, where package-private widens it only to the package the test lives in. So package-private is the default and `protected` is a stated exception, permitted when the method carries `@ApiStatus.OverrideOnly` — an extension point implementors override — or `@VisibleForTesting` — a visibility widened to create a test seam. An unmarked `protected` is reported.
The marker is necessary because package-private is not always a compliant rewrite: a `protected` member on a published abstract base whose subclasses live in other packages is unreachable if narrowed, so demanding package-private there demands a rewrite that does not compile.
This does not soften the rule. The count of *undeclared* legal forms is still zero — what a marker hands back is a choice between two documented intents, not a choice about whether to declare one. The set is hardcoded rather than configurable for the same reason: letting each project choose which annotations legitimise `protected` reintroduces exactly the drift the rule exists to prevent. `@SuppressWarnings` remains the escape for anything else.
Markers are matched by simple name, so both `@OverrideOnly` imported directly and `@ApiStatus.OverrideOnly` qualified through its outer type are recognised.
Constructors are out of scope: you do not spy a constructor, and a private one is required both by `StaticMethodsModifyStaticState`'s utility-class exception and by PMD's `UseUtilityClass`. An `@Override` method is exempt, because Java forbids narrowing an inherited visibility and a framework superclass with a `protected` hook requires a `protected` override. A `static` method is left to `StaticMethodsModifyStaticState`, which reports it first — the rules cascade, so one method yields one violation at a time with one obvious fix.
Reporting `protected` only when no subclass uses it is not possible: PMD analyses one compilation unit at a time, and that is a whole-module question. The markers exist so the question never has to be asked — a declaration is readable from a single file, which makes the check correct even across a module boundary and into a consumer's subclass.
Permitting a marked `protected` puts this rule in opposition to nothing. PMD's own `AvoidProtectedMethodInFinalClassNotExtending` and `AvoidProtectedFieldInFinalClass` fire on `protected` in a `final` class and remain correct where they fire: nothing can override in a `final` class, so `OverrideOnly` is meaningless there, and no out-of-package subclass can exist, so a test seam has no reason to widen past package-private.

rule.name: UseVisibleForTestingAnnotation
rule.message: A package-private method must be annotated ''@VisibleForTesting''.
rule.description:
A package-private method should carry `@VisibleForTesting`.
`AvoidPrivateAndProtectedMethods` makes package-private the canonical form for an internal method. This rule makes the widened visibility read as a deliberate test seam rather than a forgotten modifier — which is the only reason the wider visibility was acceptable in the first place.
The annotation is matched by **simple name**, so any declaration works: JetBrains, Guava, AndroidX and Elastic all ship a `VisibleForTesting` and all of them are markers. Matching on the name also avoids PMD's type resolution, which needs an `auxclasspath` that consumers frequently do not configure and which would make the rule silently pass when misconfigured.
Only methods are in scope — fields, constructors and nested classes are not. `@Override` methods are exempt, and so are JUnit 5 test and lifecycle methods, which are conventionally package-private and for which the annotation would be nonsense.
Note that a package-private method is stubbable only from a test in the same package and the same classloader. That holds for a standard Gradle layout and fails under JPMS with a sealed module.

rule.name: AvoidLambdaBlockBodies
rule.message: Extract this lambda''s block body into a named method.
rule.description:
A lambda body should be an expression, not a block. Logic belongs in something with a name.
A lambda block body is anonymous by construction: no test can call it, no caller can stub it, and its branches are reachable only through the pipeline that encloses it.
**A method reference is not required.** Any non-block body satisfies this rule, so a lambda that closes over a local variable stays a lambda and simply delegates. That is the whole point — requiring a method reference would be close to unusable, because a capturing lambda cannot become one at all. PMD's own `LambdaCanBeMethodReference` then converts a bare delegation the rest of the way, so the two rules compose.
An empty block is exempt: `() -> { }` has nothing to extract, and a violation nobody can act on is worse than one that is missed. A block containing only a comment is exempt for the same reason.
Logic inside an *expression* body — a ternary, a long chain — is deliberately not reported. Block-versus-expression is a syntactic proxy for "logic hiding in an anonymous place": a good proxy and a cheap one to determine, and the start rather than the whole answer.
Note one conflict with `StaticMethodsModifyStaticState`: a block lambda in a *static* field initializer extracts to a static method, which that rule then reports. Suppress it, or better, drop `static` from the field so the extracted methods become instance methods.

rule.name: AvoidAnonymousClasses
rule.message: Extract this anonymous class into a named class.
rule.description:
An anonymous class with a body should be a named class.
Its logic has no name: nothing can instantiate it, nothing can stub it. It is the less testable of the two anonymous forms — unlike a lambda it can declare several methods and carry its own fields.
This rule exists alongside `AvoidLambdaBlockBodies` because each is the other's bypass. A ban on lambda block bodies alone is escaped in one edit by rewriting the lambda as an anonymous class, and every other rule here waves that through: it is not static, its method is `public` and `@Override`, and it is not a lambda.
Two exemptions, both because the alternative is a violation nobody can act on:
- An **empty body**, where the body is the mechanism rather than a hiding place. A `TypeToken` or `TypeReference` subclass with an empty body exists precisely to create an anonymous subclass carrying a generic signature at runtime, and no rewrite preserves that. - An **enum constant body**. PMD represents one as an anonymous class, so without this the rule would report the strategy enum, which has no anonymous-free rewrite that keeps the enum. An anonymous class declared inside a method *of* an enum is still reported — only the constant's own body is exempt.

rule.name: UseStaticImports
rule.message: Statically import ''{0}'' instead of qualifying it with its type.
rule.description:
A static member reached through its declaring type should be statically imported. The import carries the owner; the code should not repeat it on every use.
**The threshold is a floor, not a ceiling.** This rule only ever says "import this". It never reports an import as unnecessary and never stops you importing a shorter name by hand, so anything below the floor is simply your call. A report you disagree with is a `@SuppressWarnings` away.
A member is reported when its simple name is longer than three characters, is not in the exclusion list, and is not contributed by two different types in the same file. Short names are left alone because the short static members of the JDK are overwhelmingly the ambiguous ones — `of`, `get`, `min`, `max`, `now`, `abs`, `sum`.
Ambiguity between owners is handled structurally, not by the exclusion list. If a file uses both `Arrays.toString` and `Objects.toString`, neither is reported and you may import one, the other, or neither. If it uses only one, the bare name is unambiguous in that file and the import line names the owner.
The exclusion list is therefore only about *uninformative* names — factory-shaped members where the member name says what it produces but not of what, leaving the class as the only thing carrying the type. Self-describing members such as `unmodifiableList`, `toList` and `groupingBy` are deliberately absent, and are reported.
Excluded exactly: `value`, `values`, `valueOf`, `from`, `empty`, `create`, `builder`, `parse`, `now`, `between`, `copyOf`, `getInstance`, `newInstance`, `INSTANCE`. Excluded by prefix at a camelCase boundary: `of…` and `from…`, so `ofSeconds` is excluded while `offer` is not. The list is fixed; suppress at the site for your own factory methods.
Violations are reported once per member per file, not once per occurrence, because one import fixes them all.
**This rule is incompatible with PMD's `TooManyStaticImports`**, which caps static imports at four. No configuration satisfies both. If you enable `category/java/codestyle.xml`, exclude that rule.

rule.name: UseTypeImports
rule.message: Import ''{0}'' instead of writing it fully qualified.
rule.description:
A fully-qualified type name used in code should be an import. The import carries the package; the code should not repeat it on every mention.
This does **not** overlap with PMD's stock `UnnecessaryFullyQualifiedName`, which sounds like it covers the same ground and does not. That rule fires only when the simple name is *already* in scope, and its fix is to drop the qualifier. Write `java.util.List` with no import and it says nothing, because the fix there is to add one. The two partition the space:
simple name already in scope -> UnnecessaryFullyQualifiedName (stock) "drop the qualifier" simple name not yet in scope -> UseTypeImports (this rule) "add an import"
So this rule stays silent on anything reachable through `java.lang`, through the current package, or through an existing import, and a project enabling both never gets two reports for one name.
If two types in one file want the same simple name, only one of them can be imported — the rule reports neither and leaves the choice to you.
A qualified nested type such as `java.util.Map.Entry` is reported without prescribing which of the two valid fixes to apply: import the nested type and write `Entry`, or import the outer type and write `Map.Entry`.
Violations are reported once per qualified name per file, not once per mention, because one import fixes them all.
